paras: The attempted lynching of Peter Gillette took place at Whitehall, Washington County, New York, on July 16, 1903, when a crowd threatened to lynch Gillette, a Black man held on a charge of assaulting a fifteen-year-old girl. The Whitehall chief of police removed him by train to the county jail at Salem, and no lynching occurred. Papers from New York to South Carolina carried the story, most as a lynching narrowly averted in a northern state, one as a lynching that had taken place.

Whitehall lay near the Vermont line at the terminus of the Champlain Canal, where, according to the New-York Tribune, canal drivers and other workers were often idle. Gillette, described as 'a negro' in most reports and 'a mulatto' in one, was said to be 28 years old and to have left the Gentry Bros. circus as a laborer when it showed at Rutland, Vermont, the previous Monday. He was accused of assaulting Hazel Chapman, the fifteen-year-old daughter of Charles Chapman of East Whitehall, while she picked berries about two miles east of the village.

Reports differ on when the alleged assault happened: Vermont papers said Wednesday afternoon, July 15, while a wire brief said Thursday morning. Farmers from the neighborhood captured Gillette as he entered the village, by one account after they 'organized a band', while the Tribune's Troy correspondent wrote that he was taken by a crowd. He was brought before Justice Davis and sent to the village lockup, and one report said he pleaded guilty at a preliminary examination.

A crowd then gathered at the lockup, and the Tribune said the mob 'became so violent' that Chief of Police Thomas A. Walker feared trouble. Walker took Gillette out a back door to the train and carried him to the county jail at Salem, about thirty miles away, and the Tribune judged that a lynching would have followed had he stayed overnight in the 'flimsy' lockup. A Rutland account said the crowd went to the jail intending to lynch the prisoner but 'could not get at him', and a later Rutland dispatch put the crowd at about two hundred men, persuaded by officers to go home.

According to the Tribune, Sheriff Austin at Salem would not allow a crowd to collect about the jail, and doctors said the girl would soon recover. No arrests of members of the crowd were reported, and no report of an indictment, trial or sentence for Gillette appears in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune headed its Troy dispatch 'Almost a Lynching. Negro, Who Admits His Crime, Saved from Mob', blamed the threats on canalmen as 'citizens say', and credited 'the sober better sense of the county' with preventing an outbreak. Its news summary the same morning described a negro charged with assaulting a little girl who 'narrowly escaped a lynching', and the next day it ran a garbled Rutland version under the headline 'Lynching Threatened in Vermont'. Vermont dailies and weeklies printed the Rutland item as 'No Lynching at Whitehall', stating the assault as fact, and short wire versions appeared in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

In South Carolina, the Lexington Dispatch printed an Albany report of 'the lynching of a negro in Washington county' under the heading 'In New York This Time', though it conceded all details were lacking. The Windham County Reformer of Brattleboro used the episode in an editorial against Vermont papers that advocated lynching, warning that mobs 'do not bother about such trifles as identification or proofs of guilt'.

Only the Albany brief in the Lexington Dispatch said a lynching had occurred; every detailed account, including the Troy and Rutland dispatches, said Gillette was jailed alive. The girl's name also varies, given as Hazel Chapman, 15, in most reports and as Ethel Chapman, 16, in a Troy dispatch printed in Pennsylvania.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Peter Gillette
bases: A crowd sought to lynch a Black prisoner held on an assault charge and was kept from him when the police chief moved him to the county jail (A2, A4, A5, A9); no one was killed, so it is an attempted lynching.

Every detailed account says Gillette escaped the crowd and was jailed at Salem or Whitehall (A1, A2, A4, A5, A8); only a details-lacking Albany brief reported a lynching (A6). A crowd of about two hundred (A5) sought to punish an accused man, but no killing occurred.

Troy (A2, A8), Rutland (A4, A5) and an unattributed wire brief (A1) independently report the capture, the assault charge and the crowd's threat; the single report of a completed lynching (A6) is contradicted by all of them.

accounts.label: Troy wire report
accounts.gist: A crowd captured Gillette; the mob grew so violent that the police chief spirited him to Salem, and a lynching would likely have followed had he stayed in the Whitehall lockup overnight.

accounts.label: Rutland reports
accounts.gist: Farmers captured the former circus laborer and jailed him at Whitehall; a crowd (about two hundred, per the Tribune) went to the jail to lynch him but could not reach him or was persuaded by officers to go home.

accounts.label: Wire brevity
accounts.gist: Gillette, 'a mulatto', pleaded guilty at a preliminary examination and was taken to Salem 'owing to the sentiment of the people'.

accounts.label: Albany dispatch
accounts.gist: Reported 'the lynching of a negro in Washington county' with all details lacking.

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'Almost a Lynching. Negro, Who Admits His Crime, Saved from Mob' treats the confession as fact, blames idle canalmen and credits 'the sober better sense of the county'.
Vermont papers headed it 'No Lynching at Whitehall. Crowd Wanted to Get Negro Who Assaulted Young Girl', stating the assault as fact.
The Alexandria Gazette and Cameron County Press ran short wire items calling the accused 'the culprit' and saying he 'narrowly escaped lynching'.
The Lexington Dispatch (S.C.) ran an unconfirmed Albany report of a lynching under the head 'In New York This Time'.
The Windham County Reformer called the attempt 'lawlessness' and warned that mobs 'do not bother about such trifles as identification or proofs of guilt'.
